rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: Kafalah's Qur'anic anchor: Yusuf's herald offers a camel-load reward and declares 'I am za'im (guarantor) for it' (12:72); 12:66 has Ya'qub demand a solemn pledge before sending Binyamin; 12:78 shows the brothers pleading substitution of one person for another.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: 12:72 is the operative verse: 'whoever brings it shall have a camel-load, and I am bound (za'im) by it.' 12:66 supplies the surrounding pledge context (Ya'qub takes a mawthiq — binding covenant — before releasing Binyamin), and 12:78 the substitution plea ('take one of us in his place'). Together the three verses give personal suretyship (kafalah bi'l-nafs and bi'l-mal) its scriptural footing, later formalized by the schools. The verses, in the translation held in the Gold Ark Library: 12:66 — “[Jacob] said, "Never will I send him with you until you give me a promise by Allah that you will bring him [back] to me, unless you should be surrounded by enemies." And when they had given their promise, he said, "Allah, over what we say, is Witness."” 12:72 — “They said, "We are missing the measure of the king. And for he who produces it is [the reward of] a camel's load, and I am responsible for it."” 12:78 — “They said, "O 'Azeez, indeed he has a father [who is] an old man, so take one of us in place of him. Indeed, we see you as a doer of good."” Why here: The Qur'an opens the Kafalah ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 12:66; 12:72; 12:78.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2295
rows.detail: The Prophet declined to lead the funeral prayer of a man who died in debt until Abu Qatada undertook the debt — then he prayed.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Salama bin Al-Akwa'. What: Two funerals are brought; for the debtor the Prophet says 'lead the prayer of your friend' and only prays after Abu Qatada declares he will settle the two dinars. The founding case for voluntary guarantee (kafalah) of another's debt. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “A dead person was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he might lead the funeral prayer for him. He asked, "Is he in debt?" When the people replied in the negative, he led the funeral prayer. Another dead person was brought and he asked, "Is he in debt?" They said, "Yes." He (refused to lead the prayer and) said, "Lead the prayer of your friend." Abu Qatada رضی اللہ عنہ said, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! I undertake to pay his debt." Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) then led his funeral prayer.” It stands in Kafalah. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2295.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2298
rows.detail: 'Whoever among the believers dies in debt, its repayment is on me' — the Prophet as guarantor of last resort once conquests brought wealth.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Abu Huraira. What: Completes the 2295 story arc: early on the Prophet refused prayer over debtors; after the conquests he declared himself responsible for any believer's unpaid debt — the state assuming the guarantor role. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Whenever a dead man in debt was brought to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) he would ask, "Has he left anything to repay his debt?" If he was informed that he had left something to repay his debts, he would offer his funeral prayer, otherwise he would tell the Muslims to offer their friend's funeral prayer. When Allah made the Prophet (ﷺ) wealthy through conquests, he said, "I am more rightful than other believers to be the guardian of the believers, so if a Muslim dies while in debt, I am responsible for the repayment of his debt, and whoever leaves wealth (after his death) it will belong to his heirs.” It stands in Kafalah. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2298.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2291
rows.detail: The Israelite loan story: 'Allah is sufficient as a surety (kafil)' — a 1,000-dinar loan made with God named as guarantor and witness, repaid miraculously by sea.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Abu Huraira. What: A man lends 1,000 dinars accepting Allah alone as kafil and witness; the debtor, unable to find passage, sends the money in a hollowed piece of wood which the sea delivers. Bukhari places it in the Kafalah chapter as the archetype of guarantee made in trust. Dated 621 CE (high confidence). The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "An Israeli man asked another Israeli to lend him one thousand Dinars. The second man required witnesses. The former replied, 'Allah is sufficient as a witness.' The second said, 'I want a surety.' The former replied, 'Allah is sufficient as a surety.' The second said, 'You are right,' and lent him the money for a certain period. The debtor went across the sea. When he finished his job, he searched for a conveyance so that he might reach in time for the repayment of the debt, but he could not find any. [...]” It stands in Kafalah. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 621 (dated record, high confidence). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2291.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2290
rows.detail: Personal sureties (kafalah bi'l-nafs) taken for an accused man until his case reached Umar — Companion-era practice of body-surety.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Hamza bin 'Amr al-Aslami. What: Umar's zakat collector Hamza takes personal sureties for an adulterer until the case comes before Umar — Bukhari's chapter evidence that guaranteeing a person's appearance (not just a debt) was practiced law in the earliest community. Dated 622-625 CE (medium confidence). The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Umar (ra) sent him (i.e. Hamza) as a Sadaqa / Zakat collector. A man had committed illegal sexual intercourse with the slave girl of his wife. Hamza took (personal) sureties for the adulterer till they came to 'Umar. 'Umar had lashed the adulterer one hundred lashes. 'Umar confirmed their claim (that the adulterer had already been punished) and excused him because of being Ignorant. Jarir Al-Ash'ath said to Ibn Mas'ud regarding renegades (i.e., those who became infidels after embracing Islam), "Let them repent and take (personal) sureties for them." They repented and their relatives stood sureties for them. [...]” It stands in Kafalah. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 622 (dated record, medium confidence). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2290.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2297
rows.detail: Ibn ad-Daghina's protection (jiwar) of Abu Bakr — tribal suretyship of a person's safety, given and later returned.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Aisha. What: When Abu Bakr set out for Ethiopia, Ibn ad-Daghina, chief of Qara, took him under his declared protection; Bukhari files it under Kafalah as guarantee of person and safety in pre-hijra Mecca. Dated 622-634 CE (medium confidence). The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Since I reached the age when I could remember things, I have seen my parents worshipping according to the right faith of Islam. Not a single day passed but Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) visited us both in the morning and in the evening. When the Muslims were persecuted, Abu Bakr رضی اللہ عنہ set out for Ethiopia as an emigrant. [...]” It stands in Kafalah. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 622 (dated record, medium confidence). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2297.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2287
rows.detail: 'Delay by a wealthy debtor is injustice; if your debt is transferred to a rich debtor, accept it' — the adjacent hawala anchor.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Abu Huraira. What: The debt-transfer (hawala) command sits in the chapter immediately before Kafalah in Bukhari; jurists treat guarantee and transfer as sibling institutions. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Procrastination (delay) in paying debts by a wealthy man is injustice. So, if your debt is transferred from your debtor to a rich debtor, you should agree.” It stands in Transferance of a Debt from One Person to Another (Al-Hawaala). Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2287.

rows.name: Sunan Abi Da'ud 3565
rows.detail: 'Al-za'im gharim' — the guarantor is liable. The legal maxim of kafalah, absent from Bukhari, carried by the Sunan.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Sunan was compiled by Abu Dawud al-Sijistani (817-889); it is the third of the six canonical Sunni hadith collections. Narrator: Abu Umamah. What: The Prophet's farewell-sermon phrase 'the borrowed is to be returned, the guarantor is liable, and debt is to be repaid' becomes the black-letter maxim of every later kafalah chapter. Graded Sahih. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “I heard the Messenger of Allah صلی ‌اللہ ‌علیہ ‌وسلم Said: Allah, Most Exalted, has appointed for everyone who has a right what is due to him, and no will be made to an heir, and a woman should not spend anything from her house except with the permission of her husband. He was asked: Even foodgrain, Messenger of Allah? He replied: That is the best of our property. He then said: A loan must be paid back, a she-camel lent for a time for milking must be returned, a debt must be discharged, one who stands surety is held responsible.” It stands in Wages (Kitab Al-Ijarah). Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sunan Abi Da'ud 3565.

rows.name: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1265
rows.detail: Tirmidhi's parallel of 'al-za'im gharim', delivered in the farewell sermon of 632 CE — dated to the year, high confidence.
rows.detail_long: Who: Jami' al-Tirmidhi is the collection of Muhammad al-Tirmidhi (824-892), a scholar of the hadith sciences known as a master of hadith analysis. Narrator: Abu Umamah. What: Same maxim as Abu Dawud 3565, independently transmitted; this narration is dated to 632 CE (farewell sermon) at high confidence — the single best-dated kafalah text. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Narrated Abu Umamah: During the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) saying during the Khutbah: The borrowed is to be returned, and the guarantor is responsible, and the debt is to be repaid. [Abu 'Eisa said:] There are narrations on this topic from Samurah, Safwan bin Umayyah, and Anas. [He said:] The Hadith of Abu Umamah is a Hasan Gharib Hadith. It has also been reported through other routes besides this, from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ).” It stands in The Book on Business. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 632 (dated record, high confidence). Source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1265.

rows.name: Ibn Abbas (attrib., Tanwir al-Miqbas)
rows.detail: The earliest attributed reading: za'im in 12:72 glossed as 'I guarantee a camel-load for him' — spoken by the youth Yusuf sent.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abd Allah ibn Abbas (618-686) was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, remembered as the 'Scholar of the Umma' and highly regarded for his knowledge of traditions and his interpretation of the Qur'an. The commentary Tanwir al-Miqbas is attributed to him by tradition; the attribution is traditional, not critical, which is why the work is marked 'attrib.' What: Tanwir al-Miqbas renders the verse: 'he who brings it shall have a camel load, and I am answerable for it — I guarantee a camel load for him.' The companion-attributed gloss that makes za'im = guarantor, the seed of the whole kafalah lineage. Attribution of this tafsir to Ibn Abbas is traditional, not critical — hence the work is 'attrib.' Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 687 (death of Ibn Abbas, to whom the work is attributed). Source: Tanwir al-Miqbas (attrib. Ibn Abbas), on Q12:72.

rows.name: al-Tabari
rows.detail: Al-Tabari collects the chains: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id b. Jubayr, Qatada and al-Dahhak all gloss za'im as kafil (guarantor); Mujahid alone reads it as 'the herald'.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abu Ja'far al-Tabari (839-923) was a Sunni scholar, historian, jurist and Qur'an commentator from Amol in Tabaristan who worked in Baghdad. He followed the Shafi'i school for nearly a decade, then developed his own school of law (the Jariri school), which lasted about two centuries after him. He is best known for his Qur'an commentary, Tafsir al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan), and his historical chronicle. What: On 12:72 he marshals numbered isnads (19543-19551): via Mu'awiya from Ibn Abbas — 'wa-ana bihi za'im, ya'ni: kafil'; likewise Sa'id b. Jubayr, Qatada (twice) and al-Dahhak, against Mujahid's minority reading of za'im as the announcer. He also surveys the qira'at of suwa' and what the king's vessel was. This is the moment the guarantor reading becomes the recorded majority position. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 923 (year of the author's death). Source: Jami' al-Bayan (Tafsir al-Tabari), on Q12:72.

rows.name: al-Qurtubi
rows.detail: Al-Qurtubi turns the verse into fiqh: seven masa'il, equating za'im = kafil = hamil = damin = qabil, and testing whether guaranteeing an unknown amount is valid.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Qurtubi (1214-1273) was an Andalusian Maliki jurist and Qur'an commentator, taught by the scholars of Cordoba; after the city fell in 1236 he moved to Egypt. His twenty-volume commentary, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an (Tafsir al-Qurtubi), is a general commentary written from a Maliki point of view. What: On 12:72 he opens seven legal questions: the synonymy 'al-za'im wa'l-kafil wa'l-hamil wa'l-damin wa'l-qabil sawa'' (guarantor terms are equivalents); whether daman of a majhul (unknown quantity — a camel-load) can bind, answered because the load was a known measure; and the verse as proof for ju'alah (reward contracts), citing al-Shafi'i's positions. The bridge from exegesis to contract law. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Kafalah ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 1273 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, on Q12:72.

rows.name: Ibn Kathir
rows.detail: Ibn Kathir narrates the bowl episode and reads 'wa-ana bihi za'im' as assurance of delivery of the promised reward.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Kathir (1301-1373) of Damascus was a Qur'an commentator, historian and scholar, an expert in tafsir, history and fiqh. A Shafi'i, he is known for a commentary that takes a critical approach to Isra'iliyyat (stories taken from earlier communities). What: On 12:72 he relates the placing of the bowl in Binyamin's bag (with Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd on what the vessel was) and closes: 'and I will be bound by it — as assurance of delivery of the reward.' The consolidating late-classical transmission. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Kafalah ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1373 (year of the author's death). Source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, on Q12:72.

rows.name: Mufti Muhammad Shafi Usmani
rows.detail: The modern tafsir layer: Shafi Usmani works through the juristic problems of 12:72 — how a prophet could stage the accusation, and the verse's use for surety and reward contracts.
rows.detail_long: Who: Mufti Muhammad Shafi Usmani (1897-1976) was born in Deoband, became chief mufti of Darul Uloom Deoband in 1931, and later Grand Mufti of Pakistan in Karachi. His best-known work, Ma'ariful Qur'an, is an Urdu commentary on the whole Qur'an that began as a decade of weekly radio lectures. He belonged to the Hanafi school and the Deobandi movement. What: On 12:72 he translates za'im as 'I stand a surety for it', then interrogates the episode's legal ethics (the staged theft charge, Benyamin's consent, al-Qurtubi's account) — a 20th-century Hanafi-Deobandi jurist reading the kafalah verse with classical tools. His son Taqi Usmani carries the same school into AAOIFI. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Kafalah ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1976 (year of the author's death). Source: Ma'ariful Quran, on Q12:72.

rows.name: al-Kasani
rows.detail: Al-Kasani systematizes kafalah in Bada'i al-Sana'i: guarantee of the person and of property, pillars, and conditions, for the Hanafi school.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kasani (d. 587 AH / 1191 CE) was a jurist of the Hanafi school and author of Bada'i al-Sana'i, a work that draws heavily on al-Sarakhsi's al-Mabsut. What: Bada'i al-Sana'i's Kitab al-Kafalah gives the Hanafi architecture: kafalah bi'l-nafs (surety for a person's appearance) versus kafalah bi'l-mal (surety for property/debt), the pillar being offer-and-acceptance, with the creditor's right running against guarantor and principal together. Death year 1191 CE from standard references. In the work itself (vol. and page 6:2; our literal translation from the Arabic): “(As for) the pillar, it is the offer and the acceptance: the offer from the guarantor and the acceptance from the claimant [creditor]. And this is according to Abu Hanifa and Muhammad, and it is the later statement of Abu Yusuf.” It also states: “And in his first statement the pillar is the offer only; (as for) the acceptance, it is not a pillar; and it is one of the two statements of al-Shafi'i.” It also states: “[From the hadith the page cites, of the funeral of a man of the Ansar:] "Is there a debt upon your companion?" It was said: yes, two dirhams or two dinars. So he refrained from praying over it.” It also states: “And because kafala is a joining in language, and an undertaking of [liability to] the claim for what is upon the principal debtor in the Law, not a conferring of ownership.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Kafalah ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1191 (death year 587 AH / 1191 CE, standard references). Source: Al-Kasani, Bada'i al-Sana'i, Kitab al-Kafalah.

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Ibn Qudama's al-Mughni (5:71) sets out kafalah for the Hanbalis: guarantee of person and of property, valid across the schools.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi (1147-1223) was a jurist of the Hanbali school who studied in Baghdad and taught in Damascus; he is regarded as one of the school's most authoritative classical figures. He is best known for al-Mughni, a legal encyclopedia that compares the opinions of the Sunni schools while setting out the Hanbali position in detail. He also wrote 'Umdat al-Fiqh. What: Al-Mughni's treatment (vol. 5, p.71 in the standard print) records the two types — daman al-mal and kafalah bi'l-nafs — their conditions, and the near-consensus of the four schools on validity, citing the Abu Qatada hadith and 'al-za'im gharim' as proofs. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Kafalah ladder, Hanbali voice; shown at 1223 (year of the author's death). Source: Ibn Qudama, al-Mughni, 5:71.

rows.name: OIC Fiqh Academy
rows.detail: OIC Fiqh Academy, 2nd Session (Jeddah, Dec 1985): no fee may be charged on an uncovered guarantee — the ruling behind today's kafalah-fee dispute.
rows.detail_long: Who: The International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC issues numbered resolutions at its sessions; AAOIFI's standards cite them. What: The Academy resolved that a guarantee (kafalah/daman) is a gratuitous contract of the tabarru' family: charging a fee for bearing another's risk is impermissible where the guarantor has no covering funds, since the fee would be compensation for pure liability — economically riba-like. Modern letters of guarantee and bank kafalah fees are structured around (and disputed under) this ruling. In the source's own words (International Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC) - Resolution No. 12 (12/2) The Letter of Guarantee): “First: It is not permissible to charge a fee for the issuance of the letter of guarantee (in which, customarily, the amount and the period of guarantee are considered) whether it is with or without a coverage.” “Second: The administrative expenses for issuing a letter of guarantee of both kinds are permissible by Shariah, provided that they do not exceed the actual costs for the services of the same kind.” “The guarantee (kafalah) is a benevolent contract motivated by grace and mercy. The jurists have decided against taking a fee for issuing guarantees” “If, on the other hand, the letter of guarantee has a cover, the relationship between the applicant of the guarantee and its issuer is that of an agency; and an agency may exist with or without a fee” Not confirmed by the source read: It does not limit the no-fee ruling to an UNCOVERED guarantee: the page prints 'whether it is with or without a coverage'. It does not use the words 'kafalah-fee dispute'. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 1985 (2nd session, Jeddah, December 1985). Source: OIC Fiqh Academy, 2nd Session (Jeddah, Dec 1985).

rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 5 (Guarantees) codifies kafalah for the industry: bank guarantees, letters of credit, documentary credits.
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS5 standardizes personal and financial guarantees for Islamic financial institutions — permitted structures, the no-fee-for-pure-guarantee rule inherited from the 1985 OIC resolution, and the documentation of letters of guarantee. Year shown as tentative 2002, pending confirmation of the exact issue year. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 2002 (tentative — 2002 pending confirmation). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 5 (Guarantees).

rows.name: Industry practice
rows.detail: Kafalah underpins trade finance, letters of guarantee and takaful structures; the guarantee-fee question remains the live dispute.
rows.detail_long: Who: This rung is a snapshot of how the contract is used in the market today. It is a description of practice, not a ruling. What: Banks issue kafalah-based letters of guarantee and standby credits daily; deposit-insurance and takaful schemes lean on the same contract. The unresolved tension is fees: the classical gratuitous-contract rule (OIC 1985) versus commercial reality, with several national boards allowing cost-based charges — contested, not settled. Why here: 'Today' rung of the Kafalah ladder; shown at 2024 (current practice window). Source: Industry practice; national Shari'ah board positions on guarantee fees.
